section-5: Ancient sources include the Vedas and Upanishads (ideas of rita - cosmic order - and dharma), the epics (the Ramayana's ideal of Ramarajya; the Shanti Parva of the Mahabharata on the duties of kings, rajadharma), the Dharmashastras (Manusmriti, Yajnavalkya Smriti), Kautilya's Arthashastra, Buddhist and Jain texts (the Buddhist idea of the 'Mahasammata' - the 'great elect' king chosen by the people - and ideas of the sangha), Ashoka's edicts and Sangam literature. Medieval sources include the writings of Barani ('Fatawa-i-Jahandari'), Abul Fazl ('Ain-i-Akbari') and Bhakti and Sufi thought.

Modern Indian political thought arose from the colonial encounter: social reformers (Rammohun Roy, Vidyasagar, Phule), religious revivalists (Dayanand, Vivekananda), nationalists (Naoroji, Gokhale, Tilak, Aurobindo, Tagore), Gandhi, Nehru, Ambedkar, Savarkar, M. N. Roy, Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan and others. Scholars such as V. R. Mehta, Thomas Pantham and Bhikhu Parekh note that Indian political thought combines indigenous traditions with Western ideas of liberalism, nationalism and socialism, adapted to Indian conditions.
section-6: The Arthashastra ('science of wealth' or 'science of polity') is attributed to Kautilya, also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta, the minister of Chandragupta Maurya (fourth century BCE), though scholars believe the text was compiled and revised over several centuries (roughly between the second century BCE and the third century CE). The text was lost for centuries and rediscovered in 1905 by R. Shamasastry, who published it in 1909 and translated it into English (1915).

It has 15 books (adhikaranas), 150 chapters and about 6,000 shlokas, covering the king's training, ministers, administration, law and justice, revenue and taxation, the economy (agriculture, trade, mining, state enterprises), espionage, foreign policy, war and military strategy. Kautilya defined Arthashastra as the science that deals with the acquisition and protection of the earth (territory). He is often compared to Machiavelli for his realism, though the Arthashastra is much more comprehensive and also emphasises the welfare of the people. Max Weber said that compared with the Arthashastra, Machiavelli's 'Prince' is harmless.
section-7: Saptanga theory (seven limbs of the state): (1) Swami - the king, the most important element; (2) Amatya - ministers and officials; (3) Janapada - territory and population; (4) Durga - fortified capital; (5) Kosha - treasury; (6) Danda - army and coercive power; and (7) Mitra - allies. The state is like an organism, and each part supports the others. Kautilya gave detailed qualities of the king: he must be of noble birth, wise, energetic, self-controlled, educated in philosophy (anvikshiki), the Vedas, economics (varta) and politics (dandaniti), and should follow a strict daily routine.

The king's duty is to protect the people and promote their welfare: 'In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare his welfare.' He must uphold dharma, maintain order (matsyanyaya - the 'law of the fish', where big fish eat small fish - would prevail without danda), administer justice, collect taxes fairly and protect the weak. The king governs with the help of a council of ministers (mantriparishad) and a large bureaucracy of superintendents (adhyakshas). The state played an active role in the economy and social welfare, making Kautilya's state a kind of welfare state.
section-8: Kautilya's foreign policy is based on the Mandala theory (circle of states): the king who seeks conquest (vijigishu) is at the centre; his immediate neighbour is a natural enemy (ari); the state beyond the enemy is a natural friend (mitra); and so on in concentric circles. The middle king (madhyama) and the neutral king (udasina) are also considered. This anticipates the realist idea of the balance of power.

Six-fold policy (shadgunya): (1) sandhi (peace or treaty); (2) vigraha (war); (3) asana (neutrality or remaining quiet); (4) yana (preparing for or marching to war); (5) samshraya (seeking protection or alliance with a stronger king); and (6) dvaidhibhava (dual policy - peace with one and war with another). Four upayas (means): sama (conciliation), dana (gifts or bribery), bheda (dissension or divide and rule) and danda (force). Kautilya also described an extensive network of spies (gudhapurushas), including disguised as ascetics, merchants and others, and types of warfare (open war, covert war and silent war). His realism makes him important for contemporary strategic studies in India.
section-9: Raja Rammohun Roy (1772-1833) is called the 'father of modern India' and the first Indian liberal. His liberalism had several dimensions: (1) religious - he founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828), advocated monotheism, rationalism and opposed idolatry and superstition; (2) social - he campaigned against sati (abolished in 1829), polygamy and caste rigidity, and for women's property rights and education; (3) educational - he supported English and scientific education (his letter to Lord Amherst, 1823) and helped found the Hindu College (1817); and (4) political - he defended freedom of the press (protesting the Press Ordinance of 1823), demanded the separation of executive and judiciary, trial by jury, Indianisation of services, protection of peasants against zamindars, and codification of laws.

He was influenced by Western liberal thinkers (Bentham, Locke), the French Revolution, and the Upanishads. He supported constitutional government and the rule of law, and believed British rule could help modernise India. Critics note that his liberalism was limited to elites and accepted colonial rule. He died in Bristol in 1833 while representing the Mughal emperor in England, and the Mughal emperor had given him the title 'Raja'.
section-10: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902), disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, preached a nationalism based on spiritual revival, pride in Indian culture and service to the poor. He believed that India's strength lay in its spirituality and that national regeneration required removing poverty, ignorance and caste oppression. He called on Indians to serve the poor as God ('daridra narayana') and said: 'So long as the millions live in hunger and ignorance, I hold every man a traitor who, having been educated at their expense, pays not the least heed to them.'

He emphasised strength, fearlessness and self-confidence ('Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached'), physical fitness and character-building education. He criticised untouchability ('don't touch-ism') and priestly domination, supported women's education and envisioned the rise of the Shudras (the working classes). His ideas inspired nationalists such as Tilak, Aurobindo, Subhas Chandra Bose and Gandhi. Critics argue that his nationalism had a Hindu emphasis, though he also respected other religions.
section-11: Vivekananda's internationalism came from the Vedantic idea of the unity of all existence (Advaita) and the oneness of humanity. At the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago (11 September 1893), he spoke of tolerance and universal acceptance, quoting the hymn: 'As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take... all lead to Thee.' He condemned sectarianism, bigotry and fanaticism.

He believed that the East could teach spirituality to the West, while the West could teach science, organisation and practical efficiency to the East - a synthesis of cultures. He founded the Vedanta Society in New York (1894) and spread Indian philosophy abroad. His idea of 'universal religion' accepted all religions as true paths. His nationalism was therefore not narrow; he saw a regenerated India contributing to world civilisation.
section-12: Gopal Krishna Gokhale (1866-1915), a leader of the Moderates, was a professor at Fergusson College (Pune), a member of the Imperial Legislative Council (from 1902), President of the Congress (Benares, 1905) and founder of the Servants of India Society (1905), which trained dedicated public workers. Gandhi called him his 'political guru'. He believed in British justice, constitutional methods, gradual reform and the 'spiritualisation of politics'.

On swadeshi, Gokhale supported the economic idea of promoting Indian industries and goods, which he considered patriotic and practical, but he opposed the boycott of British goods as a political weapon, fearing it would provoke hostility and harm moderate politics. He criticised colonial economic policies - high military expenditure, heavy land revenue, and the drain of wealth - in his budget speeches, and demanded more spending on education and Indianisation of services. He moved a bill for free and compulsory primary education (1911), which was defeated. Gokhale represents liberal, reformist, constitutional nationalism.
section-13: Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856-1920), called 'Lokmanya' and the 'father of Indian unrest' (by the British journalist Valentine Chirol), was a leader of the Extremists. He declared: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' (1916). He published the newspapers 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English), and used popular festivals - Ganapati (1893) and Shivaji (1895) festivals - to mobilise the masses.

His idea of swaraj meant self-government and, increasingly, freedom from foreign rule, based on national pride and self-reliance. Methods: swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. He was imprisoned for sedition in 1897 and in Mandalay (1908-1914), where he wrote 'Gita Rahasya', interpreting the Gita as a gospel of action (karma yoga). He founded the Home Rule League (1916) and helped negotiate the Lucknow Pact (1916). Critics note that his use of Hindu symbols may have alienated Muslims and that he opposed the Age of Consent Bill (1891), arguing that social reform should not be imposed by a foreign government.
section-14: Gandhi's concept of ahimsa (non-violence) was drawn from Jainism, Buddhism, the Bhagavad Gita, the Sermon on the Mount, Tolstoy ('The Kingdom of God Is Within You'), Ruskin ('Unto This Last') and Thoreau. For Gandhi, ahimsa was not merely the absence of violence but active love - goodwill towards all, including opponents. 'Non-violence is the greatest force at the disposal of mankind. It is mightier than the mightiest weapon of destruction.'

He distinguished between the non-violence of the brave (based on moral strength) and the non-violence of the weak (based on cowardice), and said that if he had to choose between cowardice and violence, he would choose violence. He applied non-violence to political action (non-cooperation, civil disobedience), economics (decentralised village economy, trusteeship), social reform (removal of untouchability) and international relations. Truth (satya) and non-violence were inseparable: 'Truth is God'. Gandhi's ideas influenced Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and the Dalai Lama.
section-15: Satyagraha ('truth-force' or 'soul-force') was first used by Gandhi in South Africa in 1906 against the 'Black Act' (registration law for Indians). It means holding firmly to truth and resisting evil through self-suffering, without violence or hatred, in order to convert the opponent rather than defeat him. Gandhi wrote 'Satyagraha in South Africa' and 'Hind Swaraj' (1909), where he criticised modern civilisation.

Forms of satyagraha: non-cooperation (withdrawing from unjust institutions), civil disobedience (deliberately breaking unjust laws and accepting punishment), fasting, hartal (strike), picketing, boycott and hijrat (voluntary migration). Requirements of a satyagrahi: truthfulness, non-violence, fearlessness, self-discipline, celibacy (brahmacharya), non-possession, faith in God and willingness to suffer. Satyagraha differs from passive resistance, which may be a weapon of the weak and may allow violence. Gandhi used it in Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918), Ahmedabad (1918), Non-Cooperation (1920-1922), Salt Satyagraha (1930) and Quit India (1942).
section-16: Jawaharlal Nehru (1889-1964) was influenced by Fabian socialism, Marxism and his visit to the Soviet Union (1927). In his Lucknow Congress presidential address (1936), he declared socialism as the solution to India's problems. However, he rejected violent revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat, preferring democratic socialism achieved through democratic, constitutional and peaceful means.

Features: a mixed economy, with the public sector controlling 'commanding heights' (heavy industries, infrastructure, defence) and the private sector operating in other areas (Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956); economic planning through the Planning Commission (1950) and Five-Year Plans (the Second Plan's Mahalanobis model emphasised heavy industry); land reforms; scientific temper and modern technology ('temples of modern India' - dams, steel plants); the Avadi Congress resolution (1955) for a 'socialistic pattern of society'; and welfare for the weaker sections. Critics say his socialism led to bureaucracy, inefficiency and the 'licence-permit raj', while defenders credit it with building India's industrial and scientific base.
section-17: Nehru was a staunch secularist, influenced by his rational and scientific outlook ('The Discovery of India', 1946). For him, secularism meant that the state would not identify with any religion, would treat all religions equally and guarantee freedom of religion, and that citizenship would be independent of religion. He opposed both majority and minority communalism, saying 'communalism of the majority is especially dangerous' because it can pass for nationalism.

He insisted on a secular state after Partition despite communal violence, promoted the Hindu Code Bills (1955-1956) to reform Hindu personal law, and supported minority rights. Critics argue that Nehru's secularism was Western and elitist, imposed from above on a religious society (T. N. Madan, Ashis Nandy), and that he did not apply the same reform to minority personal laws. Others (Rajeev Bhargava) defend it as a 'principled distance' model suited to India's diversity.
section-18: Dr Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891-1956), born in a Mahar (Dalit) family in Mhow, faced untouchability but earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics. His main works include 'Annihilation of Caste' (1936), 'Who Were the Shudras?' (1946), 'The Untouchables' (1948), 'The Problem of the Rupee' and 'The Buddha and His Dhamma' (1957). He founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), the Independent Labour Party (1936), the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942) and the People's Education Society (1945).

For Ambedkar, social justice meant the annihilation of caste, abolition of untouchability, equality of status and opportunity, and dignity for all. He led the Mahad satyagraha (1927) for access to public water, publicly burned the Manusmriti (1927), and fought for separate electorates for the depressed classes, but signed the Poona Pact (1932) with Gandhi, accepting reserved seats in joint electorates. As Chairman of the Drafting Committee, he ensured Fundamental Rights, abolition of untouchability (Article 17), reservations and protection for SCs and STs. He also championed women's rights through the Hindu Code Bill and resigned as Law Minister (1951) when it was delayed. He converted to Buddhism with hundreds of thousands of followers in Nagpur on 14 October 1956. He received the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1990.
section-20: The Arthashastra is a comprehensive treatise on statecraft attributed to Kautilya, minister of Chandragupta Maurya, rediscovered by R. Shamasastry (1905). Theory of the state: the Saptanga theory of seven elements - king, ministers, territory and people, fort, treasury, army and allies - presents an organic view of the state. Without danda (coercive authority), matsyanyaya would prevail. The king is the centre of the state; he must be well-trained, disciplined and devoted to the welfare of his subjects. The bureaucracy is elaborate, with superintendents for various departments; the state regulates the economy, prices, weights and measures, and provides welfare for orphans, the aged and the sick.

Law and justice: Kautilya listed four sources of law - dharma (sacred law), vyavahara (evidence, contracts), charitra (custom) and rajashasana (royal edicts), with royal edicts prevailing in case of conflict. Courts included dharmasthiya (civil) and kantakashodhana (criminal). Foreign policy: the Mandala theory (circle of states and natural enemies and friends), the six-fold policy (sandhi, vigraha, asana, yana, samshraya, dvaidhibhava) and four upayas (sama, dana, bheda, danda), along with espionage and diplomacy.

Evaluation: Kautilya is regarded as a realist thinker comparable to Machiavelli, emphasising the security and power of the state, but his concept of the king's duty to the welfare of the people gives his theory a moral dimension. Critics point to the use of espionage, deception and harsh punishments, and the absence of popular participation. His work remains important for Indian strategic thinking - India's 'Kautilya Dialogues' and the study of 'Indian strategic culture' draw on it.
section-21: Raja Rammohun Roy: liberal and rationalist; founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); opposed sati, polygamy, idolatry and caste rigidity; supported women's rights, English and scientific education, freedom of the press, rule of law, separation of powers, jury trial, Indianisation of services and protection of peasants. He combined the Upanishadic tradition with Western liberalism and is regarded as the pioneer of the Indian Renaissance and modern Indian liberalism. His limitations included faith in British rule and an elite focus.

Swami Vivekananda: spiritual nationalism, based on Vedanta, pride in India's spiritual heritage, service to the poor ('daridra narayana'), strength and fearlessness, character-building education, criticism of caste and untouchability, uplift of women and the masses, and the vision of the rise of the working people. His internationalism was based on the unity of humanity and religions, demonstrated at the Chicago Parliament (1893); he called for a synthesis of Eastern spirituality and Western science. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service.

Comparison: both were reformers who sought to regenerate Indian society; Roy emphasised reason, liberal rights and Western education, while Vivekananda emphasised spiritual revival, national pride and service. Roy worked within a liberal, constitutional framework, and Vivekananda inspired nationalism and social service. Both contributed to the intellectual awakening that prepared the ground for the national movement.
section-22: Gokhale: moderate liberal nationalist; believed in British justice and constitutional methods; criticised colonial economic policies in the Imperial Legislative Council; supported swadeshi in the economic sense but opposed boycott; advocated education (free and compulsory primary education bill, 1911), Indianisation of services, decentralisation, and the 'spiritualisation of politics' (politics as service, through the Servants of India Society). Gandhi regarded him as his guru, and Jinnah admired him as well.

Tilak: extremist or assertive nationalist; 'Swaraj is my birthright'; used religious and cultural symbols (Ganapati and Shivaji festivals) to mobilise people; advocated swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance; criticised the 'mendicancy' of moderates; was imprisoned for sedition; and interpreted the Gita as a call to action. He led the Home Rule League and the Lucknow Pact. He believed political freedom should come before social reform.

Comparison: Gokhale and Tilak, both from Maharashtra (Chitpavan Brahmins), represented two strands of nationalism - moderate (reform, gradualism, cooperation with the British, social reform first) and extremist (swaraj, mass mobilisation, self-reliance, political freedom first). The split at Surat (1907) reflected their differences. Yet both were patriots who contributed to Indian political consciousness, and Gandhi combined Gokhale's moral approach with Tilak's mass mobilisation.
section-23: Philosophy of non-violence: Gandhi's ahimsa was rooted in religious traditions (Jainism, Buddhism, Vaishnavism, the Gita, Christianity) and thinkers (Tolstoy, Ruskin, Thoreau). Non-violence is active love, the law of our species, and inseparable from truth; it requires courage, self-suffering and respect for the opponent. Ends and means are inseparable - impure means cannot produce pure ends ('the means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree').

Satyagraha in practice: developed in South Africa (1906-1914); applied in Champaran (indigo farmers, 1917), Kheda (peasants, 1918), Ahmedabad (mill workers, 1918), the Rowlatt satyagraha (1919), Non-Cooperation (1920-1922), Bardoli (1928, under Vallabhbhai Patel), the Salt Satyagraha and Civil Disobedience (1930-1934), individual satyagraha (1940) and Quit India (1942). Methods included non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting, hartal, boycott and constructive work (khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability, prohibition, village industries, basic education).

Evaluation: Gandhi made non-violent mass resistance a powerful political weapon, mobilising millions, including women and peasants, and influencing civil rights movements worldwide. Critics argue that he suspended movements abruptly (Chauri Chaura), that his religious idiom alienated some Muslims, that his approach to caste was reformist rather than radical (Ambedkar's criticism), and that non-violence may not work against ruthless regimes. Nevertheless, his ideas remain relevant to conflict resolution, environmentalism and ethical politics.
section-24: Nehru's socialism: influenced by Fabians, Marxism and the Soviet experience, but committed to democracy and civil liberties; democratic socialism through a mixed economy, public sector dominance in key industries, economic planning (Planning Commission, Five-Year Plans), land reforms, and the 'socialistic pattern of society' (Avadi, 1955). He emphasised industrialisation, science and technology (IITs, atomic energy, space research), self-reliance and the welfare of the poor. The Directive Principles reflect these ideas.

Nehru's secularism: the state should not be associated with any religion; equal respect and freedom for all religions; equal citizenship; opposition to all forms of communalism; reform of Hindu personal law; protection of minorities. He saw secularism as essential for national unity in a diverse society, especially after Partition.

Nation-building and evaluation: Nehru combined socialism, secularism, democracy and non-alignment as the four pillars of his vision for postcolonial India. Achievements: democratic institutions, industrial and scientific base, secular state and India's international standing. Criticisms: inefficiency and slow growth of the planned economy ('Hindu rate of growth'), bureaucratic controls, neglect of agriculture and primary education, the 1962 China war, and a top-down secularism. After 1991, India moved away from Nehruvian socialism towards liberalisation, but his ideas still shape debates.
section-25: Critique of caste: Ambedkar argued that caste is a system of 'graded inequality' based on endogamy and sanctioned by Hindu scriptures (Manusmriti); it divides labourers, not just labour; it destroys public spirit, fraternity and morality. In 'Annihilation of Caste' (1936), he called for the destruction of the religious notions on which caste is based, inter-caste marriage and inter-dining. He criticised Gandhi's approach (reforming caste while retaining varna) as inadequate.

Political democracy and social democracy: Ambedkar insisted that political democracy (one person, one vote) must be accompanied by social and economic democracy, based on liberty, equality and fraternity. In his speech of 25 November 1949, he warned of the 'life of contradictions' and urged constitutional methods, warning against hero-worship. He supported a strong Centre, fundamental rights, judicial remedies (Article 32), reservations, and a parliamentary system. He supported state socialism in 'States and Minorities' (1947), proposing state ownership of key industries and agriculture.

Legacy: Ambedkar's thought inspired Dalit movements, the BSP, reservation policies, and the struggle for social justice. His conversion to Buddhism (1956) symbolised a rejection of caste hierarchy. He also contributed to labour laws, women's rights (the Hindu Code Bill), economic policy (influencing the creation of the Reserve Bank of India and the Finance Commission) and water and power planning. Today, he is seen as one of the most important thinkers of modern India, and his birthday (14 April) is celebrated as Ambedkar Jayanti.
section-28: Determinants: (1) geography - India's size, location in the Indian Ocean at the crossroads of Asia, land borders with China, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, the Himalayas and sea lanes; (2) history and culture - the legacy of the freedom struggle, anti-colonialism, Gandhian non-violence, and civilisational links with Asia; (3) security - threats from Pakistan and China, terrorism, insurgency; (4) economic needs - development, trade, investment, technology, energy security (India imports over 80 percent of its oil); (5) domestic politics - public opinion, parties, coalition partners, states (for example, Tamil Nadu on Sri Lanka, West Bengal on the Teesta waters); (6) leadership - the vision of leaders like Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Rao, Vajpayee and Modi; and (7) the international environment - the Cold War, the post-Cold War order, globalisation and the rise of China.

Institutions involved include the Prime Minister's Office, the Ministry of External Affairs, the National Security Council (1998), the Ministry of Defence and intelligence agencies, with Parliament exercising some oversight. Article 51 of the Constitution (DPSP) directs the state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations, respect international law and settle disputes by arbitration.
section-29: Principles: (1) Panchsheel (1954) - mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence; (2) non-alignment and, later, strategic autonomy and multi-alignment; (3) anti-colonialism and anti-racism (opposition to apartheid); (4) peaceful settlement of disputes; (5) support for the UN and multilateralism; (6) nuclear disarmament (while keeping India's nuclear option); (7) 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' (the world is one family), the theme of India's G20 presidency (2023); and (8) South-South cooperation.

Other doctrines include the Gujral Doctrine (1996-1997), which said India should give concessions to small neighbours without expecting reciprocity; 'Neighbourhood First' (2014); SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region, 2015) in the Indian Ocean; and 'Act East'. India's policy combines idealism (peace, cooperation) with realism (security, national interest).
section-30: Objectives: protection of national security, sovereignty and territorial integrity; economic development through trade, investment, technology transfer, energy and food security; a peaceful and stable neighbourhood; promotion of international peace and a just world order; protection of the interests of the Indian diaspora (over 3.5 crore people of Indian origin and NRIs) and their welfare; enhancing India's global standing, including a permanent seat in the UN Security Council; combating terrorism; and addressing global issues such as climate change, pandemics and maritime security.

Foreign policy also seeks to promote India's soft power - yoga (International Day of Yoga, 21 June, since 2015), culture, Buddhism, Bollywood and democracy - and to lead the Global South (Voice of the Global South Summits, 2023; the inclusion of the African Union in the G20 during India's presidency).
section-31: Non-alignment was developed by Nehru and expressed in his speech of 7 September 1946: 'We propose, as far as possible, to keep away from the power politics of groups, aligned against one another.' It did not mean neutrality, isolation or passivity; it meant freedom to judge each issue on merit, independent foreign policy, peaceful coexistence and opposition to military blocs. India played a key role in founding NAM (Belgrade, 1961).

Reasons for non-alignment: to protect newly won independence, to focus on economic development, to receive aid from both blocs, to promote world peace and to maintain India's moral leadership. India's non-alignment was tested by the 1962 war with China (when it sought Western help) and the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty of Friendship. After the Cold War, non-alignment evolved into 'strategic autonomy' and 'multi-alignment' - partnerships with the USA, Russia, Japan, the EU, Israel, the Gulf states and others, and membership of groups such as BRICS, SCO and the Quad simultaneously. India's position on the Russia-Ukraine war (abstentions at the UN while calling for dialogue) reflects this approach.
section-32: Development: Homi Bhabha led the atomic energy programme (Atomic Energy Commission, 1948). India refused to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), calling it discriminatory because it divided the world into 'nuclear haves' (five recognised states) and 'have-nots'. India conducted a 'peaceful nuclear explosion' at Pokhran ('Smiling Buddha', 18 May 1974) under Indira Gandhi, and five tests in May 1998 ('Operation Shakti') under Vajpayee, declaring itself a nuclear weapon state. Pakistan tested soon after. India also refused to sign the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT, 1996).

Nuclear doctrine (2003): credible minimum deterrence; no-first-use policy, with nuclear weapons used only in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or forces anywhere (and possibly against major biological or chemical attacks); massive retaliation causing unacceptable damage; civilian political control through the Nuclear Command Authority; no use against non-nuclear states; a moratorium on nuclear tests; and continued commitment to global, verifiable nuclear disarmament (Rajiv Gandhi's Action Plan at the UN, 1988). India has developed a nuclear triad (land, air and sea-based delivery - INS Arihant submarine, 2016). India became a member of the Missile Technology Control Regime (2016), Wassenaar Arrangement (2017) and Australia Group (2018), but its entry to the Nuclear Suppliers Group has been blocked by China.
section-33: Phases: (1) 1947-1991 - limited cooperation, with tensions over US alliances with Pakistan (SEATO, CENTO), the US 'tilt' towards Pakistan in 1971 (USS Enterprise sent to the Bay of Bengal), India's non-alignment and friendship with the USSR, and US sanctions after 1974; there was cooperation during the 1962 war and the Green Revolution (US food aid, PL-480). (2) 1991-2000 - improved relations after economic reforms; sanctions after the 1998 tests; Clinton's visit (2000). (3) 2000-present - strategic partnership: the Next Steps in Strategic Partnership (2004), the civil nuclear deal (2005-2008), defence agreements (LEMOA 2016, COMCASA 2018, BECA 2020 - the 'foundational agreements'), designation of India as a 'Major Defence Partner' (2016), the Quad (India, USA, Japan, Australia, revived in 2017), iCET (Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology, 2023), and growing trade (the USA is India's largest trading partner).

Issues of disagreement: trade disputes and tariffs (the USA imposed high tariffs on Indian goods in 2025), H-1B visas and immigration, India's purchase of Russian weapons (S-400) and oil, the CAATSA sanctions law, human rights criticism, and differences on Iran, climate and WTO issues. Both countries are democracies with shared concerns about China's rise and the Indo-Pacific, and the Indian diaspora in the USA is influential.
section-34: The India-US Civil Nuclear Agreement was announced in a joint statement by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush on 18 July 2005 and signed as the '123 Agreement' (named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act) in October 2008, after the US Congress passed the Henry J. Hyde Act (2006). India agreed to separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities, place civilian facilities under International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards, sign an Additional Protocol, maintain its moratorium on testing and strengthen export controls.

The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) granted India a 'clean waiver' in September 2008, allowing nuclear trade despite India not having signed the NPT - recognising India as a responsible nuclear power. The deal ended India's nuclear isolation and allowed it to import uranium and reactors (agreements followed with France, Russia, Canada, Australia, Kazakhstan, Japan and others). It faced opposition in India: the Left parties withdrew support from the UPA government, which survived a confidence vote in July 2008. Implementation has been slow due to India's Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (2010), which foreign suppliers found restrictive.
section-35: Indo-Soviet relations grew from the 1950s: Soviet support for India on Kashmir in the UN Security Council (vetoes), aid for heavy industries (the Bhilai steel plant), mediation at Tashkent (1966) after the India-Pakistan war, and the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (August 1971), which helped India in the Bangladesh war. The USSR was India's main supplier of weapons and technology (MiG fighters, tanks, submarines).

After the Soviet collapse, India and Russia signed a new treaty (1993) and the Declaration on Strategic Partnership (2000), upgraded to a 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership' (2010). Cooperation includes defence (S-400 air defence system, BrahMos missile joint venture, Sukhoi Su-30MKI fighters, INS Vikramaditya aircraft carrier, AK-203 rifles), nuclear energy (the Kudankulam nuclear power plant), space (training of Indian astronauts for Gaganyaan), energy (India's large imports of Russian oil after 2022), annual summits and multilateral forums (BRICS, SCO, RIC). Challenges include Russia's closer ties with China and Pakistan, India's growing ties with the USA, Western sanctions on Russia, payment problems and the war in Ukraine, on which India has called for dialogue and diplomacy.
section-36: Phases: (1) friendship - India was among the first non-communist countries to recognise the People's Republic (1950); the Panchsheel Agreement (1954) on trade with Tibet; 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'. (2) Conflict - China's control of Tibet (1950), the Dalai Lama's flight to India (1959) and the border war (October-November 1962), in which China defeated India and occupied Aksai Chin. Relations remained frozen until ambassadors returned in 1976. (3) Normalisation - Rajiv Gandhi's visit (1988), the Agreements on Peace and Tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) (1993, 1996), Vajpayee's visit (2003), the Special Representatives mechanism for the boundary question, and the Wuhan (2018) and Mamallapuram (2019) informal summits.

China became one of India's largest trading partners, but with a huge trade deficit (over 80 billion US dollars in 2023-2024). Both cooperate in BRICS, SCO, AIIB and on climate issues. After the Galwan clash (June 2020), relations deteriorated sharply; India banned many Chinese apps and restricted investments. Disengagement agreements at several friction points followed, and in October 2024 an agreement on patrolling in Depsang and Demchok led to further normalisation, including the resumption of direct flights and the Kailash Mansarovar yatra in 2025.
section-37: (1) The boundary dispute: about 3,488 km of disputed border along the LAC - the western sector (Aksai Chin, occupied by China, claimed by India as part of Ladakh), the middle sector (Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand) and the eastern sector (Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as 'South Tibet', rejecting the McMahon Line of 1914). Clashes include 1962, Nathu La (1967), Sumdorong Chu (1986-1987), the Depsang (2013), Chumar (2014) and Doklam (2017, in the India-Bhutan-China trijunction) standoffs, the Galwan clash (15 June 2020, 20 Indian soldiers killed), and Yangtse (Tawang, 2022).

(2) Tibet and the Dalai Lama (living in Dharamshala since 1959). (3) China's close relationship with Pakistan ('all-weather friendship'), including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, which India opposes, and China's blocking of UN listings of Pakistani terrorists (until Masood Azhar was listed in 2019). (4) China's growing presence in South Asia and the Indian Ocean (the 'string of pearls' - ports in Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Myanmar and Bangladesh; the Belt and Road Initiative, which India has not joined). (5) China's opposition to India's NSG membership and UN Security Council permanent seat. (6) River waters (Chinese dams on the Brahmaputra/Yarlung Tsangpo, including the large Medog project announced in 2024-2025). (7) The trade deficit and economic dependence. (8) Stapled visas for residents of Arunachal and renaming of places in Arunachal by China.
section-38: Wars and conflicts: 1947-1948 (Kashmir war after tribal invasion, ceasefire under UN auspices and the creation of the Line of Control); 1965 (ended by the Tashkent Agreement, 1966); 1971 (Bangladesh liberation war; 93,000 Pakistani soldiers surrendered; the Simla Agreement, 1972, committed both to bilateral resolution of disputes and converted the ceasefire line into the Line of Control); Siachen (1984); Kargil (1999); and military crises after terrorist attacks (the Parliament attack, 2001-2002 - Operation Parakram; Mumbai, 2008; Uri, 2016, leading to 'surgical strikes'; Pulwama, 2019, leading to the Balakot air strike; and the Pahalgam attack in April 2025, which led to 'Operation Sindoor' strikes on terrorist sites in Pakistan in May 2025, followed by a ceasefire).

Peace efforts: the Indus Waters Treaty (1960, brokered by the World Bank; India placed it 'in abeyance' in April 2025); the Lahore bus journey and Declaration (Vajpayee and Nawaz Sharif, 1999); the Agra Summit (2001); the Composite Dialogue (2004-2008); and confidence-building measures (the Kartarpur Corridor, 2019). Key issues: Kashmir (especially after India revoked Article 370 in 2019, which Pakistan protested), cross-border terrorism (India demands that Pakistan stop supporting groups like Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed), Siachen, Sir Creek, water sharing and nuclear risks. Trade and people-to-people contacts remain minimal.
section-39: Sri Lanka is separated from India by the narrow Palk Strait (about 30 km). Ties include Buddhism (Ashoka's son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitra), the Ramayana, culture, trade and the Tamil population. The ethnic conflict between the Sinhala majority and the Tamil minority arose from policies such as the 'Sinhala Only Act' (1956), discrimination in education and jobs, and anti-Tamil riots (1983, 'Black July'). The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), led by V. Prabhakaran, fought for a separate Tamil state (Eelam). The civil war ended with the LTTE's defeat in May 2009.

Other issues include fishermen arrested for crossing into each other's waters, the Katchatheevu island (ceded to Sri Lanka in 1974), Chinese influence (Hambantota port leased to China for 99 years in 2017), and the 13th Amendment to Sri Lanka's Constitution (devolution to provinces). India provided about 4 billion US dollars in assistance during Sri Lanka's economic crisis (2022). Cooperation includes trade (the India-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement, 1998, in force 2000), development projects, energy and connectivity.
section-40: The Indo-Sri Lanka Accord was signed in Colombo on 29 July 1987 by Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and President J. R. Jayewardene. Provisions: Sri Lanka would devolve power to provinces through provincial councils (implemented by the 13th Amendment to the Sri Lankan Constitution, 1987), temporarily merge the Northern and Eastern provinces (Tamil-majority areas) subject to a referendum, recognise Tamil as an official language, grant amnesty to militants, and ensure that its territory and ports would not be used by foreign military powers against India's interests. Militant groups would surrender their weapons, and India would help ensure this.

The Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) was sent to enforce the accord. The LTTE initially accepted but later refused to disarm and fought the IPKF. Sinhala nationalists (the JVP) also opposed the accord, leading to violent unrest. A Sinhalese naval rating attacked Rajiv Gandhi during the guard of honour in Colombo. The accord's devolution provisions have been only partly implemented; the merger of the provinces was struck down by Sri Lanka's Supreme Court (2006).
section-41: The IPKF was deployed in Sri Lanka from July 1987 to March 1990, peaking at about 100,000 troops. Its mission was to disarm Tamil militant groups and maintain peace. When the LTTE refused to disarm, the IPKF fought it in the Jaffna peninsula and the north and east (Operation Pawan, October 1987), facing difficult guerrilla warfare. About 1,200 Indian soldiers were killed and thousands injured.

The IPKF faced opposition from both the LTTE and the Sri Lankan government of President Ranasinghe Premadasa, who demanded its withdrawal and even secretly supplied weapons to the LTTE. It was withdrawn in March 1990 under Prime Minister V. P. Singh. The LTTE assassinated Rajiv Gandhi at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on 21 May 1991, partly in revenge for the IPKF intervention. The IPKF experience is often called 'India's Vietnam', and it made India cautious about direct military intervention in neighbouring conflicts.
section-42: India played a decisive role in Bangladesh's liberation (1971), supporting the Mukti Bahini and accepting about 10 million refugees. Relations have had ups and downs depending on governments in Dhaka (close under the Awami League, more strained under military rule and the BNP). Achievements: the Ganga Water Treaty (1996, for 30 years); the Land Boundary Agreement (1974, implemented in 2015 through India's 100th Constitutional Amendment, exchanging 111 Indian enclaves for 51 Bangladeshi enclaves and settling the boundary); the maritime boundary settlement through arbitration (2014); connectivity projects (bus and rail links, the Maitree Express, Akhaura-Agartala rail link, use of Chittagong and Mongla ports for transit to Northeast India); power supply; and trade (Bangladesh is India's largest trading partner in South Asia).

Issues: illegal migration and border management (the 4,096 km border, the longest India shares with any country, including with Mizoram); border killings by security forces; sharing of the Teesta waters (an agreement has been held up by West Bengal's objections); insurgent groups (Bangladesh under Sheikh Hasina cracked down on Northeast Indian insurgents); and Chinese influence. After Sheikh Hasina was ousted by student-led protests in August 2024 and fled to India, relations with the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus became strained, with concerns about the safety of minorities.
section-43: India and Myanmar share a 1,643 km border with Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram (Mizoram shares about 510 km). Historical links include Buddhism, British rule (Burma was part of British India until 1937), and the Indian community. Myanmar is India's gateway to Southeast Asia and a member of ASEAN and BIMSTEC. India initially supported democracy (Aung San Suu Kyi received the Nehru Award in 1993) but from the mid-1990s engaged with the military regime for security and strategic reasons, especially to counter insurgents and Chinese influence.

Projects: the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project (connecting Kolkata to Sittwe port in Myanmar by sea, then by river and road to Mizoram, through Paletwa and Zorinpui), the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway (from Moreh in Manipur to Mae Sot in Thailand), and the Rhi-Tiddim road and Tamu-Kalewa road. Issues: insurgent camps in Myanmar (India conducted cross-border strikes in 2015); drug trafficking from the Golden Triangle; the Rohingya crisis; Chinese influence; the Free Movement Regime (allowing border residents to move 16 km into each other's territory without visas, which India decided in 2024 to end and fence the border, opposed by Mizoram and Nagaland); and the impact of the February 2021 military coup, after which over 30,000 Chin refugees fled to Mizoram, where they were sheltered by the state government and civil society because of ethnic kinship.
section-44: The Look East Policy was launched in 1991-1992 by Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao after the end of the Cold War, the collapse of the Soviet Union (India's major partner) and the economic crisis that led to liberalisation. Its aims were to develop economic and strategic ties with Southeast Asia (especially ASEAN) and East Asia (Japan, South Korea, China), which had experienced rapid growth, to attract investment and trade, and to counter China's influence.

Phases: in the first phase (1990s), the focus was on ASEAN and economic ties - India became an ASEAN sectoral dialogue partner (1992), full dialogue partner (1996), member of the ASEAN Regional Forum (1996) and summit-level partner (2002). The second phase (from 2003) extended the policy to Japan, South Korea, China and Australia, including security cooperation, free trade agreements (the ASEAN-India FTA in goods, 2010; CEPAs with Singapore 2005, South Korea 2010, Japan 2011) and the East Asia Summit (2005). The policy also aimed to develop Northeast India through connectivity with Southeast Asia.
section-45: Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the Act East Policy at the ASEAN-India Summit in Myanmar in November 2014, signalling a more active and action-oriented approach. Its '4 Cs' are Culture, Commerce, Connectivity and Capacity building; later also described with 3 Cs (Commerce, Culture and Connectivity). It extends to the wider Indo-Pacific, including Japan, South Korea, Australia and the Pacific Islands (the Forum for India-Pacific Islands Cooperation, FIPIC, 2014).

Key features: strategic partnerships with Japan (the 'Special Strategic and Global Partnership'), Australia, Vietnam, Indonesia and others; defence cooperation and naval exercises (Malabar, with the USA, Japan and Australia); the Quad; connectivity projects through the Northeast (the Kaladan project, the Trilateral Highway, the Agartala-Akhaura rail link, the Bangladesh-Bhutan-India-Nepal (BBIN) motor vehicle agreement); the ASEAN-India Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2022); BIMSTEC; cultural links (Buddhist circuits, Ramayana festivals); and the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (2019). For Mizoram and the Northeast, Act East offers opportunities for trade and development, but implementation has been slow and the 2021 Myanmar coup has affected projects.
section-46: India's strengths: the world's most populous country (about 1.43 billion, overtaking China in 2023) with a young population (demographic dividend); the fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP and third-largest by purchasing power parity, with growth of around 6-8 percent; a nuclear-armed state with the world's second-largest army and growing navy; a strong space programme (Mangalyaan 2014, Chandrayaan-3 landing near the Moon's south pole in 2023, Aditya-L1 solar mission); IT and pharmaceutical industries ('pharmacy of the world', supplying COVID-19 vaccines through 'Vaccine Maitri'); democracy and soft power; a large diaspora; and active diplomacy (G20 presidency 2023, membership of BRICS, SCO and the Quad, leadership of the Global South).

Challenges: poverty, inequality and unemployment; low per capita income (about 2,500-2,700 US dollars); inadequate health and education; infrastructure gaps; border disputes with China and Pakistan; terrorism and internal security; dependence on imports of energy and defence equipment (though 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' aims at self-reliance); and the lack of a permanent seat in the UN Security Council. Experts describe India as an 'emerging' or 'leading' power aspiring to become a developed nation by 2047 ('Viksit Bharat').
section-48: Determinants: geography (size, location in the Indian Ocean, borders with China and Pakistan, the Himalayas, maritime trade routes), history (colonial experience, freedom struggle, Partition), culture and values (Gandhian non-violence, civilisational heritage, tolerance), economic needs (development, energy security, technology, investment), national security (borders, terrorism), domestic politics (public opinion, parties, coalition pressures, states' interests), leadership (Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Rao, Vajpayee, Manmohan Singh, Modi) and the international environment (Cold War, globalisation, rise of China, US-China rivalry).

Principles and objectives: Panchsheel; non-alignment and strategic autonomy; anti-colonialism and anti-racism; peaceful settlement of disputes; support for the UN and multilateralism; nuclear disarmament with credible minimum deterrence; Neighbourhood First and Act East; SAGAR; and Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam. Objectives include security and territorial integrity, economic development, a peaceful neighbourhood, a just world order, protection of the diaspora, greater global influence (UN Security Council seat) and leadership of the Global South.

Evolution: Nehru's idealist non-alignment (1947-1964); Indira Gandhi's realism (1971 war, Indo-Soviet treaty, 1974 nuclear test); Rajiv Gandhi's outreach (China visit, IPKF); post-1991 pragmatism (Look East, economic diplomacy, the 1998 tests, ties with the USA and Israel); and the post-2014 assertive and multi-aligned approach (Act East, Quad, neighbourhood first, strategic autonomy). Foreign policy thus combines enduring national interests with adaptation to changing global conditions.
section-49: Non-alignment: proposed by Nehru (1946) and formalised through NAM (1961); meant independence from Cold War blocs, freedom to decide on merits, peaceful coexistence and support for decolonisation. It enabled India to obtain aid from both sides, focus on development, play a mediating role (Korea, Indochina, Suez) and lead the developing world. It was tested by the 1962 war with China and the 1971 Indo-Soviet treaty. Critics said India's non-alignment leaned towards the USSR. After the Cold War, it evolved into 'strategic autonomy' and 'multi-alignment', as reflected in partnerships with the USA, Russia, Japan, the EU and the Gulf.

Nuclear policy: from Bhabha's atomic energy programme and Nehru's support for disarmament (he proposed a ban on nuclear tests in 1954) to the 1974 Pokhran test, the refusal to sign the NPT (1968) and the CTBT (1996) as discriminatory, and the 1998 tests declaring India a nuclear weapon state. The 2003 doctrine provides for credible minimum deterrence, no first use, massive retaliation and civilian control. The India-US nuclear deal (2005-2008) and the NSG waiver (2008) ended India's nuclear isolation. India continues to support universal, non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament.

Connection: both non-alignment and nuclear policy reflect India's desire for strategic autonomy - independence in decision-making, refusal to accept a subordinate position in the international order, and protection of national security. India's nuclear weapons were justified by threats from China (which tested in 1964) and Pakistan.
section-50: India-US: from Cold War tensions (US alliance with Pakistan, the 1971 crisis, sanctions after 1974 and 1998) to a comprehensive global strategic partnership (2020). Milestones: the post-1991 economic engagement; Clinton's visit (2000); the 2005 defence framework; the civil nuclear deal (2008); foundational defence agreements (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA); the 'Major Defence Partner' status (2016); the Quad; iCET (2023); and the USA becoming India's largest trading partner. Cooperation covers defence, counter-terrorism, technology, space (NASA-ISRO), energy, education and the Indo-Pacific. Differences: trade and tariffs, visas, Russia (S-400, oil imports), human rights criticism, and different approaches to Iran and multilateral trade.

India-Russia: a 'special and privileged strategic partnership' built on decades of trust - Soviet support on Kashmir, the 1971 treaty, defence supplies (still a major share of India's equipment), BrahMos missiles, Kudankulam nuclear plant, space cooperation and energy (India became a major buyer of Russian oil after 2022). Challenges: Russia's growing closeness with China, Western sanctions, payment issues, delays in defence supplies and India's diversification of arms imports towards the USA, France and Israel.

Balancing: India pursues good relations with both powers, refusing to choose sides; this is visible in its membership of both the Quad (with the USA) and BRICS/SCO (with Russia and China), and its abstention in UN votes on the Ukraine war while calling for peace. This reflects strategic autonomy in a multipolar world.
section-51: India-China: from early friendship (Panchsheel, 1954) to the 1962 war, and a long freeze; normalisation from 1988 (Rajiv Gandhi's visit) with border peace agreements (1993, 1996, 2005, 2013), trade growth and cooperation in BRICS and SCO. Tensions: the unsettled boundary (Aksai Chin, Arunachal Pradesh), standoffs (Depsang, Doklam) and the Galwan clash (2020); China-Pakistan partnership and CPEC; Chinese presence in South Asia and the Indian Ocean; the trade deficit; Tibet and the Dalai Lama; opposition to India's NSG and UNSC aspirations; and Brahmaputra dams. India's response includes infrastructure along the border, military modernisation, economic restrictions on Chinese companies and partnerships through the Quad. Disengagement and patrolling agreements in 2024 eased tensions.

India-Pakistan: Partition and the Kashmir issue led to wars in 1947-1948, 1965, 1971 (Bangladesh) and 1999 (Kargil); the Simla Agreement (1972) committed both to bilateralism; cross-border terrorism (Parliament attack 2001, Mumbai 2008, Uri 2016, Pulwama 2019, Pahalgam 2025) led to Indian military responses (surgical strikes, Balakot, Operation Sindoor); peace initiatives (Lahore 1999, Agra 2001, Composite Dialogue, Kartarpur corridor) have repeatedly broken down. India's revocation of Article 370 (2019) and the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (2025) added new tensions. Nuclear weapons make conflict dangerous.

Significance: China is India's main strategic challenge and also a major economic partner, while Pakistan is the principal source of cross-border terrorism and military confrontation. The 'two-front' challenge shapes India's defence planning and its partnerships with other powers.
section-52: Sri Lanka: close geographical, cultural and religious ties; the Tamil ethnic conflict affected relations; India trained and supported Tamil militants in the early 1980s, then signed the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord (1987) and deployed the IPKF (1987-1990), which fought the LTTE and withdrew after heavy losses; Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by the LTTE (1991). Since then, India has followed a cautious approach, supporting devolution (13th Amendment) and reconstruction, providing large economic assistance during the 2022 crisis, and competing with China's influence (Hambantota port). Fishermen's disputes and Katchatheevu remain issues.

Bangladesh: India helped Bangladesh's liberation (1971); relations improved notably with the Land Boundary Agreement (2015), maritime settlement (2014), the Ganga Water Treaty (1996), connectivity (transit through Chittagong and Mongla ports, rail and bus links), energy and trade; issues include illegal migration, border management, Teesta water sharing and Chinese influence. The fall of Sheikh Hasina's government (2024) created new uncertainty. Myanmar: a land bridge to Southeast Asia; the shared border with four Northeast states; cooperation on counter-insurgency, the Kaladan project and the Trilateral Highway; concerns over the 2021 coup, Rohingya refugees, drug trafficking, Chinese influence and refugees in Mizoram.

Significance: India's 'Neighbourhood First' policy aims to build a peaceful, prosperous and connected neighbourhood through connectivity, trade, development assistance and people-to-people ties, while managing ethnic conflicts and the influence of China. The Northeast, including Mizoram, is directly affected by relations with Bangladesh and Myanmar.
section-53: Look East (1991-2014): launched by P. V. Narasimha Rao to engage ASEAN and East Asia economically after the Cold War and India's economic reforms; India became an ASEAN dialogue partner (1996) and summit partner (2002), joined the ASEAN Regional Forum and the East Asia Summit, and signed FTAs and CEPAs. The second phase expanded to strategic cooperation with Japan, South Korea and Australia. Act East (from 2014): Narendra Modi's more active policy with emphasis on connectivity (Kaladan, Trilateral Highway, Northeast development), commerce, culture and capacity-building, security cooperation (Quad, Malabar exercises, Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative) and strategic partnerships with Japan, Vietnam, Indonesia, Singapore and Australia.

India as a global power: strengths include population and demographic dividend, a large and growing economy, military and nuclear capabilities, space and technology, democracy, soft power, diaspora and active diplomacy (G20 presidency 2023, BRICS expansion, Global South leadership, UN peacekeeping). India seeks a permanent seat in the UN Security Council and a multipolar world order.

Challenges: poverty, unemployment, inequality, human development gaps, infrastructure deficits, dependence on imports, border threats from China and Pakistan, internal security issues and limited influence over global institutions. India's global role depends on both domestic capability (economic growth, social development, institutional strength) and effective external strategy (managing great-power relations, neighbourhood and regional leadership).
section-56: The legislature (from Latin 'legis', law) is the organ that makes, amends and repeals laws; it represents the people and is regarded as the most important organ in a democracy. Functions: (1) legislative - making laws; (2) financial - approving the budget, taxes and expenditure; (3) control over the executive - through questions, debates, motions, committees and votes of no confidence (in parliamentary systems) or impeachment, approval of appointments and treaties (in presidential systems); (4) deliberative - discussing public issues; (5) constituent - amending the constitution; (6) electoral - electing officials (in India, the President and Vice-President); (7) judicial - impeachment of the President or judges; and (8) representative - expressing public opinion and grievances.

Lord Bryce and others spoke of the 'decline of legislatures' in the twentieth century due to the growth of executive power, party discipline, delegated legislation, the complexity of issues and the role of the media. Parliamentary committees and the opposition remain important for accountability.
section-57: A unicameral legislature has one house - examples include China, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, New Zealand (since 1951), Israel and most Indian states (only six states - Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh - have Legislative Councils). Mizoram's Legislative Assembly is unicameral. Advantages: cheaper, simpler, quicker decisions, clear responsibility and no deadlocks.

A bicameral legislature has two houses - a lower house (usually directly elected, representing the people) and an upper house (representing states, regions, special interests or experience). Examples: India (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), the UK (House of Commons and House of Lords), the USA (House of Representatives and Senate), France, Japan and Australia. Advantages: revision of hasty legislation, representation of federal units (important in federations), inclusion of experts, and checking the lower house. Disadvantages: delay, cost, deadlocks and possible undemocratic composition of the upper house. Abbé Sieyès said: 'If a second chamber agrees with the first, it is superfluous; if it disagrees, it is mischievous.'
section-58: The executive (from Latin 'exsequi', to carry out) implements laws, conducts administration, maintains law and order, conducts foreign relations and defence, prepares the budget, appoints officials and exercises some legislative and judicial powers (ordinances, pardons). It includes the political executive (president, prime minister, ministers, elected for limited terms) and the permanent executive (civil servants, bureaucracy, who remain in office).

In the twentieth century, the executive has grown in power because of the welfare state, economic planning, wars and emergencies, technology and the need for quick decisions. This has led to concerns about executive dominance and the need for checks such as legislative control, judicial review, independent institutions and a free press.
section-59: Types of executive: (1) nominal (titular) and real executive - in parliamentary systems, the head of state (British monarch, Indian President) is nominal, while the Prime Minister and Cabinet are real; (2) single and plural executive - in the USA, power is vested in one person (the President), while Switzerland has a plural, collegial Federal Council of seven members; (3) parliamentary and presidential executive - the parliamentary executive is responsible to the legislature, while the presidential executive is independent of it; (4) hereditary and elected executive - monarchs inherit their position; presidents and prime ministers are elected or chosen; and (5) political and permanent executive.

Some countries have a semi-presidential (dual) executive, in which a directly elected president shares power with a prime minister responsible to parliament - for example, France (the Fifth Republic, 1958), Russia and Sri Lanka. When the president and prime minister are from different parties in France, it is called 'cohabitation'.
section-60: The judiciary interprets laws, settles disputes between individuals, between individuals and the state, and between governments (in federations), protects rights and liberties, and acts as the guardian of the constitution through judicial review. Other functions include advisory opinions (the Indian Supreme Court under Article 143), issuing writs, punishing contempt, supervising lower courts and, in some cases, judicial legislation through precedents (judge-made law in common-law systems).

Independence of the judiciary is essential and is ensured by methods of appointment (merit-based, not political), security of tenure, fixed salaries not reduced during tenure, difficult removal procedures, separation from the executive, prohibition of practice after retirement and immunity from criticism of judicial decisions (contempt power). Judicial activism refers to courts taking an active role in protecting rights and public interest (India's PIL); judicial restraint refers to courts deferring to the legislature and executive. Concerns include delays, pendency, cost of justice and accountability of judges.
section-61: In a unitary system, all powers are vested in a central government, which may create, abolish or change local and regional governments and delegate powers to them by ordinary law. Examples: the United Kingdom (with devolution to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, which Parliament could legally revoke), France, Japan, China, Italy, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Most countries in the world are unitary.

Merits: uniformity of laws and policies, strong and efficient government, quick decision-making, especially in emergencies, less expense, national unity and clear responsibility. Demerits: concentration of power can lead to authoritarianism; the central government may neglect local needs and diversity; overburdened central administration; less local participation; and unsuitable for large, diverse countries. Decentralisation and devolution help address these problems.
section-62: Characteristics: (1) a single, supreme central government; (2) local governments are created by and subordinate to the central government, which can change their powers; (3) the constitution may be written or unwritten and is often flexible; (4) single citizenship; (5) usually a single legislature (though it may be bicameral) with full law-making powers; (6) an integrated administrative and judicial system; and (7) no constitutional division of powers between the centre and regions.

In practice, many unitary states practise decentralisation (deconcentration of administration, delegation to local bodies, or devolution of legislative powers). For example, the UK's devolved assemblies have significant powers, France created regional governments (1982), and Japan has prefectures with local autonomy. Thus unitary and federal systems lie on a continuum.
section-63: The term 'federal' comes from the Latin 'foedus', meaning treaty or agreement. K. C. Wheare ('Federal Government', 1946) defined the federal principle as 'the method of dividing powers so that the general and regional governments are each, within a sphere, coordinate and independent'. Federations may be formed by 'coming together' (independent states uniting, such as the USA, Switzerland and Australia) or by 'holding together' (a large unitary state dividing power among regions to accommodate diversity, such as India, Belgium and Spain - Alfred Stepan's distinction).

Examples include the USA, Canada, Australia, Switzerland, Germany, Russia, Brazil, Nigeria and India. Merits: accommodation of diversity, protection of regional identities, decentralisation, local participation, prevention of tyranny and suitability for large countries. Demerits: weaker central government, duplication and expense, conflicts between centre and units, inequality between regions and possible secessionism.
section-64: Essential features: (1) a division of powers between the central and regional governments by the constitution (in lists or enumerated powers); (2) a written constitution that defines this division; (3) a rigid constitution, so that the division cannot be changed by one level alone; (4) supremacy of the constitution; (5) an independent judiciary to interpret the constitution and settle disputes between governments; (6) a bicameral legislature, with the upper house representing the units (such as the US Senate with equal representation of states); and (7) dual government, with citizens subject to both levels; some federations, like the USA, have dual citizenship.

Other features include fiscal federalism (division of taxing powers and grants), intergovernmental institutions (councils, conferences), and in some cases asymmetric arrangements (special status for certain units, as in India's Article 371 provisions). Federalism may be 'dual' (separate spheres) or 'cooperative' (shared responsibilities and joint programmes).
section-65: The parliamentary system originated in Britain, evolving from the eighteenth century (Robert Walpole as the first Prime Minister) and through the nineteenth century as the monarch's powers passed to the Cabinet and Parliament. It is also called the 'Westminster model' or 'cabinet government' or 'responsible government'. It is followed in India, Japan, Canada, Australia, Germany, Italy, Israel, Bangladesh and many others.

Its basic principle is the fusion of the executive and legislature: the executive (Cabinet) is drawn from the legislature, sits in it, leads it and depends on its confidence. The government can be removed by a vote of no confidence, and the executive can dissolve the lower house and call early elections. Walter Bagehot described the Cabinet as the 'hyphen' or 'buckle' joining the legislature and executive.
section-66: Features: (1) a nominal head of state (monarch or president) and a real executive (prime minister and council of ministers); (2) close relationship between executive and legislature - ministers are members of parliament; (3) majority party rule - the leader of the majority party becomes prime minister; (4) collective responsibility of the cabinet to the lower house; (5) individual responsibility of ministers; (6) leadership of the prime minister; (7) secrecy of cabinet proceedings; (8) dissolution of the lower house on the advice of the prime minister; (9) a recognised opposition (the 'government in waiting', with a shadow cabinet in Britain); and (10) political homogeneity of the cabinet (members usually from the same party or coalition).

Merits: harmony between executive and legislature; responsible government, as the executive can be questioned and removed; flexibility to change governments in emergencies without waiting for elections; representation of diverse groups in the cabinet; and political education through debates. Demerits: instability in multi-party and coalition situations (as in Italy and India in the 1990s); cabinet dictatorship when a party has a large majority; violation of the separation of powers; lack of expertise among ministers; and party discipline that weakens parliament.
section-67: The presidential system is based on the separation of powers. The USA is the classic example (since 1789); others include most Latin American countries (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina), Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Nigeria. The president is the head of state and head of government, elected directly or through an electoral college for a fixed term, and cannot normally be removed by the legislature except through impeachment for serious offences.

The president appoints cabinet secretaries, who are not members of the legislature and are responsible to the president, not to the legislature. The legislature cannot be dissolved by the president. Each branch has its own sphere, and checks and balances prevent one branch from dominating the others.
section-68: Features: (1) single executive - the president combines the roles of head of state and head of government; (2) separation of powers - the executive, legislature and judiciary are separate; members of one cannot be members of another; (3) fixed tenure of the president (four years in the USA) and the legislature; (4) the president is not responsible to the legislature, and the cabinet is responsible to the president; (5) checks and balances - presidential veto, legislative approval of appointments and treaties, control of funds, impeachment and judicial review; (6) the president cannot dissolve the legislature; and (7) the president is elected by the people (directly or indirectly), giving independent legitimacy.

Merits: stability (fixed terms), strong and decisive leadership, protection of liberty through separation of powers, the president can appoint experts as secretaries, and less dependence on party politics. Demerits: deadlock and conflict between the executive and legislature ('gridlock'), especially in divided government; rigidity (an unpopular or incompetent president cannot easily be removed); concentration of power in one person, possibly leading to authoritarianism (as in some Latin American and African countries); and less accountability between elections. Comparing the two, Juan Linz argued that parliamentary systems are more stable for new democracies, while others point to successful presidential democracies.
section-69: Democracy is government in which supreme power is vested in the people and exercised by them directly or through elected representatives, under free elections. Key elements include popular sovereignty, political equality, majority rule with minority rights, rule of law, fundamental rights, free and fair elections, accountability, independent judiciary, free press and multi-party competition.

Democracy is also a social and economic order based on equality, and a way of life based on tolerance, cooperation and respect for the individual. Contemporary theories include liberal democracy, elitist democracy (Schumpeter), pluralist democracy (Dahl), participatory democracy, deliberative democracy and social democracy. The spread of democracy has occurred in 'waves' (Huntington): the first wave (1828-1926), second wave (after 1945) and third wave (from 1974, in southern Europe, Latin America, Asia and Eastern Europe).
section-70: Direct democracy originated in ancient Athens, where adult male citizens met in the Assembly to make laws, decide war and peace and elect officials, many chosen by lot. Modern forms include the Swiss Landsgemeinde (open-air assemblies in two cantons), New England town meetings in the USA, and in India, the gram sabha, which consists of all registered voters of a village panchayat area (Article 243A).

Devices of direct democracy in modern representative systems: referendum (voters approve or reject laws or constitutional amendments), initiative (voters propose laws), recall (voters remove elected officials before their term ends) and plebiscite (a vote on a major political question such as sovereignty or territory). Merits: direct expression of popular will, political education, legitimacy. Demerits: impractical for large states, complex issues reduced to simple choices, possibility of manipulation and majority tyranny.
section-71: Representative democracy developed in Britain and the USA and is the form used by almost all modern democracies. The people elect representatives through periodic elections, and the representatives make laws and policies. Representatives are accountable to the voters, who can replace them at the next election. J. S. Mill considered it the 'ideally best form of government'.

Electoral systems: first-past-the-post (simple majority in single-member constituencies - India, UK, USA, Canada), proportional representation (party list systems - Netherlands, Israel; single transferable vote - Ireland; used in India for the Rajya Sabha and presidential elections) and mixed systems (Germany, Japan, New Zealand). Problems include the gap between representatives and citizens, the influence of money and lobbying, party control and low participation between elections; solutions include decentralisation, participatory mechanisms and transparency.
section-72: Merits of democracy: (1) based on the principle of equality and dignity of every individual; (2) government is accountable and responsive to the people; (3) protection of rights and liberties; (4) peaceful transfer of power through elections, avoiding violent revolution; (5) political education and participation of citizens; (6) better decision-making through discussion and consultation; (7) promotes patriotism and a sense of ownership among citizens; (8) accommodation of diversity and resolution of conflicts; (9) legitimacy and stability; and (10) Amartya Sen observed that no major famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press, because governments must respond to public pressure.

Democracies also tend to have better human rights records, are less likely to go to war with each other (democratic peace theory) and allow correction of mistakes through free debate and elections. Churchill's famous remark sums up the case: democracy is the worst form of government except for all others that have been tried.
section-73: Demerits or criticisms: (1) rule of the ignorant and incompetent - Plato and Aristotle feared rule by the uneducated masses; (2) 'rule of quantity, not quality' - votes are counted, not weighed; (3) slow decision-making; (4) expensive elections and the influence of money; (5) party politics, factionalism and corruption; (6) populism - politicians may make unrealistic promises and adopt short-term policies; (7) tyranny of the majority (Tocqueville, Mill) and neglect of minorities; (8) instability with frequent changes of government in coalition systems; (9) manipulation through propaganda, misinformation and social media; and (10) elitist critics (Pareto, Mosca, Michels) argue that real power remains with a small elite even in democracies.

Marxists criticise 'bourgeois democracy' as serving the capitalist class. Many of these problems can be reduced through education, electoral reforms, strong institutions, a free press and protection of rights.
section-74: Dictatorship is a form of government in which power is concentrated in a single person or a small group, who rule without effective constitutional limits, accountability to the people or genuine elections. The term comes from the Roman 'dictator', a temporary magistrate given absolute power in emergencies for six months. Modern dictatorships include Hitler's Germany, Mussolini's Italy, Stalin's USSR, Franco's Spain, Pinochet's Chile, Idi Amin's Uganda and current authoritarian regimes such as North Korea.

Features: concentration of power in one leader or party; absence or suppression of opposition parties; control of the press and media; restriction of fundamental rights and civil liberties; use of force, secret police and propaganda; one ideology imposed on society; no peaceful method of changing the government; and often a personality cult. Scholars distinguish authoritarian regimes (which control politics but allow some private freedom) from totalitarian regimes (which seek total control over all aspects of life, as described by Hannah Arendt and Carl Friedrich).
section-75: Types: (1) personal dictatorship - power held by one individual (Saddam Hussein in Iraq, Muammar Gaddafi in Libya, Idi Amin in Uganda); (2) military dictatorship - rule by the armed forces after a coup (Pakistan under Ayub Khan, Zia-ul-Haq and Musharraf; Myanmar under the junta, including after 2021; Chile under Pinochet; many African and Latin American countries); (3) single-party dictatorship - rule by one party (the Communist Party in the USSR, China, Vietnam, Cuba and North Korea; the Nazi party in Germany); (4) fascist dictatorship - extreme nationalism and totalitarian control (Mussolini, Hitler); and (5) theocratic dictatorship - rule by religious leaders (Iran's system has elements of this; the Taliban in Afghanistan).

Other forms include monarchical absolutism (Saudi Arabia), 'competitive authoritarianism' or 'hybrid regimes' that hold elections but manipulate them (as described by Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way), and 'benevolent dictatorship', a ruler who claims to rule for the good of the people (sometimes said of Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore, though it held elections).
section-76: Arguments made in favour of dictatorship: (1) quick and decisive decision-making without lengthy debates; (2) strong and stable government; (3) efficient administration and implementation of policies; (4) effective handling of emergencies, wars and crises; (5) rapid economic development (examples cited include South Korea under Park Chung-hee and China's growth); (6) national unity and discipline; (7) less expensive than democracy (no elections); and (8) leaders may be more competent than elected politicians.

However, these claims are questionable.
